utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-03-68-T, the prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness? And the second thing -- yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you're going to finish with this witness today, Mr. Di Fazio? Before he comes in. Because yesterday you showed a certain kind of -- and I can quite understand, as I said, ambivalence especially since we did not interfere at any time. But it's up to you. We certainly will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think I understand that, Your Honours. Yes. I don't think I'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But I ask that you not be surprised if I abruptly end during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, I think, Mr. Jones, we have to -- at this point we have to play it by the ear and keep both options open with the VW section, as we did yesterday. Do you agree? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, by the end of the session today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would like to make a submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. It will be short and limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. So we'll stop five minutes -- Registrar, please remind me to stop five to ten minutes before the end of the sitting with this witness so that we discuss something. Yes. Madam Usher has probably already gone to fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope you are rested enough, and we will now proceed with the cross-examination. We will make an effort to try and finish today, but I'm not promising you that because much depends on the way you answer questions, which could prolong the cross-examination until Monday. So, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ademovic. Mr. Ademovic, I want to ask you some more questions about the local independent groups and the way that they did or did not relate to each other. You said on Tuesday, the 25th of October, this week, that all the groups were independent and they did not act jointly, and you also said that nobody trusted anyone else. And you further expanded on that when you answered a question from Judge Eser regarding that issue, and you said that there was distrust between group leaders because they believed that they were the best ones to preserve their own villages, to look after their own villages. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area of Susnjari, there were three groups, three of us: My group, the Jaglici group, and the Brezova Njiva group. Each of us had our own group. If you look at the map -- if you look at the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to look at the map, Mr. Ademovic. I want to ask you this: Do you recall your evidence that the groups, the leaders, mistrusted -- the groups mistrusted each other and the leaders of these independent local groups believed they were the best ones to look after the concerns and interests of their village? Simple question. Do you remember what you said last Tuesday? That's all. Yes or no, do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this distrust that you have mentioned continue throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the intensity of the fighting developed, trust was built up because it became evident that we had to cooperate. But everybody was the best one to defend their own village. You would probably defend your own house best, just as I defended mine and they defended theirs. Those were the beginnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And -- and local knowledge, when you're underarmed, is really a very important tool to have when you're fighting a technologically superior enemy, isn't it? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not leading a fight. I was not conducting the fighting. I was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I understand. You're being attacked and you're defending. I understand that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my yard. I didn't go anywhere outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So by about what time would you say that the groups -- and I'm really talking about your area and Susnjari, the Jaglici and the third group that you mentioned whose name I've -- I can't recall at the moment, something Njiva, I think, those three groups, they eventually started to trust each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As time went by and as the attacks intensified, we did build up mutual confidence and we did assist each other, but we remained three groups. There were three different group leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I hear what you say. By what time would -- would you say in 1992 that you'd reached a position where you trusted each other?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the intensity of the attacks increased and when the numbers of refugees grew to several thousand, then willy-nilly we had to cooperate and help those people. Practically, it was a large group of refugees, and there was no longer any accommodation in houses, sheds, barns, stables. People had to stay outside. And there was hunger generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you say that this point was reached in about May of 1992, the point where you're forced to -- or you realised that you must cooperate?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mid-May, June, July. That was when the intensity of the attacks was highest. In June or July, we already had several thousand refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. But would you say that this notion that you had to cooperate, the independent local groups had to cooperate, this understanding was in place by May of 1992? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In May it was still independent activity. We would occasionally meet, exchange information, but each group was independent. There was no firm trust. I repeat, nobody believed somebody else could defend their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll return to the point at which trust built up, but I just want to go now to the original -- sorry, to an earlier point of time when there was this mistrust that you, that you have told us about. Is it your -- are you saying that there was mistrust between the local groups in April of 1992, early April and early May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, that was when I arrived up there. I said on the 18th of April, I put myself at the disposal. On the 18th of April, I arrived there and put myself at their disposal. Nobody knew what was going to happen, what the situation was going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On Tuesday the 25th of October, Madam Vidovic asked you this series of questions and you provided this series of answers: "Q. Besides this group of yours which you said was armed and which you led in the Susnjari area, were there any other armed groups within the circle that you drew?" Talking about the circle on the map. "Q. Were there people in Jaglici, Brezova Njiva?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 15 of them and ten in Brezova Njiva. In Babuljica --" I'm sorry, I'm not sure if I pronounced it correctly -- "there were about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And these groups, did they act jointly with your group?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you describe your relationship to these groups? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all independent. Nobody trusted anyone else. Everyone guarded their own village, their own house. It was such a situation that nobody ever knew whether they would see the night alive or see the morning alive." Now, to use your words, "nobody trusted anyone else," when did that atmosphere of mistrust exist? Was it in April of 1992 and early May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in April and in early May. It was only in June and July, when the number of refugees grew, when this whole area became flooded with refugees, when we were forced willy-nilly to look after these refugees. Of course then we started to cooperate better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Susnjari is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Susnjari is not at all far from Jaglici and the other small village that you mentioned, is it? They're all actually quite close to each other. If you look at the map, they all appear to be very close to each other. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that on the map. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And they're all Muslim villages, aren't they? You agree?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with one Serb house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And they're all surrounded by a hostile Serb enemy. You agree?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I indicated the villages quite correctly on the map, and you can see what the situation is if you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You did that very well. And they're all surrounded by a hostile Serb enemy. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So -- and the people in Susnjari and Jaglici, for example, knew each other quite well, didn't they? Villagers living in close proximity, same ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you find it peculiar that in those circumstances where they are people who are living close together, the same ethnic group, find themselves in the same dire situation with the same common interests, that they mistrust each other, that they don't cooperate? Was that peculiar to you back in April and early May of 1992? Did it strike you as peculiar?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would it seem peculiar? If they were cut off from each other by constant shelling. On the 18th of April the intensity of shelling - that's 1992 - it started at 10.05, the first shelling, and a large number of shells of various calibres, fired from Vratinci, landed in the Potocari area as well as in the Susnjari area. Even the cattle were shelled, and even if people wanted to cooperate, they had no opportunity, because if hundreds of shells land in a single area in a single day, or thousands of shells land in a single day, people aren't able to walk about and to sit down with each other and have coffee and talk. This is not good for people. It gives rise to fear. You can evaluate that for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In early -- sorry, in April and early May of 1992, were the people from your village, Susnjari, able to communicate with Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. Only at night. But even then, people went about very rarely at night because whenever anybody moved, there was shelling. They even shelled cattle. They instilled fear right at the beginning because they were able to do that. From the village of Lisine, they had their observers and they controlled every metre of territory. So how could one go out and risk his life? That made it impossible to communicate. You can look at the map. I don't object at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And there was no let-up in the shelling, was there? You wouldn't say that, would you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally. Occasionally there would be a lull, and then people would go back to their farms, and then again there would be both selective and non-selective shelling in every area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the lull periods, did you as the leader of the Susnjari group ever say to yourself or consider going across to Jaglici and saying to the group over there, "Let's pool our resources so that we can better resist the enemy"? Did you ever consider that? "The few resources that we have."

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the village. I was outside the village. My area was Ravni Buljim. That is between Jaglici and Brezova Njiva. You can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've got the map here. Did you ever consider going from Ravni Buljim to Jaglici -- sorry, to Susnjari and getting the Susnjari group together and then going over to speak to the lads in Jaglici and discussing possible cooperation in order to better resist the enemy? To do away with this idea of local independent groups so that you might better resist the enemy? Did you ever consider that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that where I was with my group was Ravni Buljim. The group from Jaglici was in Rupoglav. Look at the map. The geographical area of Brezova Njiva was covered by a third group so that we were around the edges of our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All the three groups were around the edges of your area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't wait for the enemy in my own house. I would go in front of house. Those are our farms. That was our area. I wouldn't wait for him inside my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can understand that. I can understand that. And it makes good sense, doesn't it, what you did, just to try and set up a line and protect your villages. That makes good sense.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it made sense or not, it was the only thing to do. This was my turf, my backyard, and I was protecting it. I was protecting my home, my family, and my friends, and so were they. Would you do the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And when you were setting up this line to protect your own backyard and your house and your -- and your family, were you acting together in cooperation with these other groups from the other villages?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the map. Everyone -- well, look at the map. If I divide this desk into three areas, I'm active in one area, the second group in the second area, the third group in the third area, and it all makes up a whole. So look at Ravni Buljim and the other two areas. There's no need for me to explain if you understand the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's move on. You -- you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, because he -- after all of this series of questions we still haven't got an answer to the basic question that you put to the witness, whether at any time he thought it fit to approach the other two groups to coordinate. He hasn't answered that question as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll revisit the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you want to revisit the issue, please do. If you don't, move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question again: Did you, in April or May 1992, consider saying to the other groups in the area, "Let us work together in defending ourselves against this technologically superior Serb enemy"? Did you ever consider that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late May and early June, and also July, as I said, when the mass of refugees grew to several thousand, I think I said quite clearly that coordination and cooperation among the groups started. I said that a long time ago. So cooperation did begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And how did that cooperation begin? Was there a discussion about it? Did you sit down with the other leaders of the other groups and talk to them about the best way to deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First we discussed how to accommodate those people, what the best way was, and that was when we began to link up the line. That's what I've been saying all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. So you actually discussed with the other leaders the need to start cooperating and working together, and that was at sometime in early June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said late May, early June, and in July when the mass of refugees grew to several thousand and accommodating and looking after those people required cooperation. And then we also began cooperating along the line, around the periphery of our area. We didn't fight among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you did. When this cooperation amongst the groups began to take place, manifest itself, did the groups consider setting up a command structure amongst these groups that were now cooperating so that they might be led together?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What command structure? What are you talking about, my dear sir? Look at this area. I do apologise, but look at what I've been saying these three days. Were there any elements or any prerequisites for a command structure? How --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I'm not talking about giving yourselves ranks like field marshals and carrying out parade drills or anything like that. I understand the situation that you were in. I understand that, okay? But what I'm asking you is this: Did you, as the cooperation between the groups developed, did the groups decide that they needed to have someone who was in charge who was going to be able to make decisions that affected all of the men in those -- those different groups? That's all I'm asking. That's what I mean by "command structure."

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I repeat, please look at what I said. Was there time? Was there room? Were there conditions for anything of that sort? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So by the time this cooperation was established and the three groups were -- and the village groups in your area were cooperating in order to maintain the line, there was no overall leader or group of men - it doesn't have to be one man, but a group of men - who were in charge of all of the men in the three groups. That never emerged, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everyone was responsible for his own group. And as for the refugees, we helped each other. Those who had more room would take refugees in. Do you know what it would mean to be the leader or the commander, to have people and soldiers come to you and say, "I have no clothing. I have no footwear. I have no this, no that"? Do you know what kind of logistic support one would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So if during this period of time when cooperation had overcome the mistrust and the groups were working and holding the line, it was possible for any one group to simply leave the line, if it so decided, and to do something else; or it was possible for one particular group to disagree with another group as to what particular manoeuvre or action should be adopted on any given day in order to maintain the line. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it was not mandatory to be a member of the group. In my earlier testimony these three days I spoke to that effect. Whatever need arose for an attack in June or July -- or, rather, when there was an attack on the refugees moving in the direction of Konjevic Polje, of course there was movement across Djermani, Jezestica to Ravna Gora to fight the Serbian forces, to protect those miserable people who were massacred down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me. Can the witness be shown P25. Just before the witness is shown that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, would you -- Mr. Ademovic. Mr. Ademovic, would you agree with me that it would have been desirable for these groups to have a command structure?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been telling you all along that there were only groups, and in my area, up until the 8th or 9th or 10th of August --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've heard what you said. It's a simple question: Would it have been desirable to have a command structure in these groups, any sort of command structure? Would it have been a good idea in the circumstances, do you think?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. There was no possibility to put something like that in place because we had to fight for our survival. I told you that in this period of time I ate such quantities of grass that would exceed by ten times my own weight. And we had the refugees there to take care of. What sort command structure would we be setting up when we were cut off, when we didn't have any bread to eat for ten months?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I hope you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you. Please look at P25. I want to read into the record the first paragraph -- two paragraphs. Follow my words: "After the action on the 21st of April, 1992, carried out in Potocari, 14 members of the Arkan unit were killed, and somebody himself was wounded and later succumbed to his wounds."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, we're not able to find this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither can I. Can you bring the document here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There's something wrong with our exhibit system. We've got a document here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. Is it possible to have it on Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It is, if Your Honours bear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because then we can simplify it. It is on Sanction now, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But this is not the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what we were seeing on the ELMO in any case and it's not what you were reading. Yes, he said P25, but what he was reading does not match what we saw here. Can I have a look at it, please? It's not. Mr. Di Fazio, let's not waste time. What you were reading is not from what appears to us to be P25. It must be from some other document. Arkan's men are not mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've been proceeding on the basis -- it's a mistake, it's not just my mistake. It says Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes. What could be the problem -- isn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The document I'm interested in is a document dated the 23rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is neither 26 nor 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. The document I'm interested in is the 23rd of June. It's a report to the republican TO staff, signed by the -- by Mr. Oric, signed on the 23rd of June, sent on the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P25 is definitely purported to be signed by Naser Oric, but it's not the one you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you give us a moment, if Your Honours, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm not angry at you, Mr. Di Fazio. These things happen. But of course we need to see the documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. P269, apparently. And may I see it before it's given to the witness. My document, if Your Honours -- is stamped with what appears to be official court document, saying P25. So obviously there's been some sort of mistake somewhere in the past and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was not on the list of the exhibits. We don't have it here with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not make a major issue out of it. If it was a mistake, let's try to find a solution. I understand, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is the one, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 269 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's 269. No question. We've got the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because we don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry about that. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to be on Sanction or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We're trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. At least let's have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think we can start again. Mr. Ademovic, you see the first paragraph that I started to read out earlier, and it continues: "Until the 20th of May, several successful actions were carried out on the territory of Srebrenica municipality. All those actions were carried out without proper coordination, since all representatives of authorities before the onset of the war had left the territory of Srebrenica, including the then Srebrenica TO command, and many of them found refuge in Serbia. "Since there was evident need for coordination of all actions on the territory of Srebrenica municipality, the organisers of previous actions met on the 20th of May, 1992, in the village of Bajramovici and made the decision to form a Crisis Staff of Srebrenica TO, which would include Zulfo Tursunovic, Akif Ustic, Becir Bogilovic, Naser Oric, Hamdija Fejzic, Sevket Djozic and Ahmo Tihic." Now, this document, if your turn to the second page, is apparently signed by Mr. Oric. Now, if those are the words of Mr. Oric, would you agree that that makes good sense, the sentiments contained in that paragraph, that there wasn't any proper coordination and the representatives -- there wasn't proper coordination and, therefore, there was a decision to meet and form a Crisis Staff; in other words, a sort of leadership. Would you agree with that? Does that make good sense?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't see any date, or, rather, it is not clearly visible. I see 03/06/19, but I can't see -- I can't make out the year entered into the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If there's any problem with the dates, Madam Vidovic will ask you about it. But I'm not asking you about the dates of the document, I'm asking you about the content. Would you agree with these words: "There was an evident need for coordination of all actions on the territory of Srebrenica municipality"? Would you agree that there was such a need back then in 1992? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you no. I heard about such documents for the first time in Nijaz Masic's book. And as far as the signature is concerned, if I may be allowed to further explain. Look at the signature and look at the stamp. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please look at the signature and the stamp. I hold you in high esteem. You have far more experience than I do, although I have some experience in graphics. Look at the way in which the stamp was used here. I believe that you know what the rules for the use of the stamp are. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. You tell us about the stamp. You tell us all about it.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules governing the use of stamps in administration. That's what I meant. This is pure forgery. You probably got this from the project bureau, just as I did when there was this trumped-up document bearing the name, I believe it was, of Milko Markovic, involving me. And I noticed this bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So you can instantly tell that that's a forgery, can't you, just by looking at it? Straight away you can tell it's a forgery.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of a document bears no validity for me. I never saw anything of the sort. There were no circumstances in place for this, and I never heard of anything of this sort until I read it in Nijaz Masic's book. I believe I told you so already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, let's look at the content of this fake, this forgery. Do you agree with the content of this forgery; namely, that there was a definite need for coordination of all actions on the territory of Srebrenica municipality? Would you agree with that, forgery or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I told you nobody even pondered any sort of coordination. Everybody took care of their own turf and had so many things on their minds rather than walking ten or 15 kilometres away. Do you think that Srebrenica was a free territory? It was cut off into different enclaves. It looked like leopard skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. I've finished with that document, Madam Usher, thank you. If -- the scenario that you've been describing regarding the workings of these local independent groups in your area and their relationship with each other and the way they functioned, was that happening on more or less the same basis all across the Srebrenica area, the area throughout Srebrenica municipality where there were Muslim -- Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consider this, I believe I made myself quite clear: Look at what I marked on the map. Look at the map, please. It was only on the 10th of August 1992, that I was able to look out into the world. The door finally opened for me. Before that, I was in encirclement. How was I able to know what was going on elsewhere? In that particular period of time probably something similar was going on there to what was going on in my area. But I could only imagine what was going on in Potocari. It was only later that I realised that everything had been razed. You can go to Potocari now and look at the traces of what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So what I was asking was, essentially, using all of the knowledge that you have since 1992, anything that you -- any knowledge that you might have acquired afterwards from talking to people, discussing the war, thinking back on those events and those times, can you say that this development of local independent groups, the scenario that you've described happening in your area, was it happening over the wider Srebrenica area amongst the Muslim villages, the same -- the same pattern; the emergence of local groups that did -- that coordinated with each other from time to time, if they chose, and didn't at other times?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was able to get in touch after the 10th of August, 1992, in Potocari, Lehovici, I realised that I had experienced some of the things that other groups in those areas had experienced, and that was only normal because that was the only way for us to survive. Now, how did they make do? Probably the same way as I did. On the 10th of August, 1992 -- or, rather, before that date I did not have an opportunity to know anything about it. It was when I started receiving information about what was going on in the other areas from the refugees who came from different directions that I realised that I had been experiencing similar things - these refugees were coming from the areas covered by the other groups - that there had been massacre -- they had been massacred, people killed and taken away. This was confirmed later on in Suha and Repovci. And you want to deny all that, that all that had happened. These are the things that I have in mind when I talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on to Motorolas. Your Motorola was a police Motorola, had a range of four to five kilometres, correct, in good country? I'm sure you can answer that with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one that I had, it was hand-held with a range of four to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And of course if the territory was rugged, then the range would have been less if there were any obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you've told the Trial Chamber that you could hear what the Serb military was doing and also what it intended doing. That was, wasn't it --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- an invaluable tool that produced invaluable material, namely intelligence about what the Serbs were up to; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was of little value, but I was able to obtain very good and valuable information through it. In 1992, the police equipment was already outdated and quite unsophisticated compared to what the Yugoslav People's Army had, just to make this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Don't worry. I'm not suggesting that you had better equipment than the Serbs. I'm not going to make that suggestion, okay? All I'm asking you is this: It was invaluable material that was produced, namely intelligence. Okay? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I obtained through the little Motorola I had helped save thousands of people. In fact, it saved my own life. And not only mine but that of dozens of people who were passing through. I was able to warn them to seek shelter away from the clearings, the meadows, and so on. Although in spite of that, many of them were killed and massacred. I had to use axes to cut off the limbs of those who were wounded, without any medications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you share the intelligence that you obtained from listening on your radio with the other groups that were operating in your area? The ones that were holding the line, as you described?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at my position up there at Ravni Buljim. If the intelligence had to do with Jaglici or Rupoglav, which was about a kilometre from where I was, wouldn't you yourself find it necessary to get in touch with the people over there and warn them? Because if they get to be destroyed, so will I be. Of course, I had to take care as to what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You started sharing intelligence with the other groups and letting them know what the Serbs were up to; right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you put in place a system for making sure that the intelligence that you got, you obtained, was disseminated through to the other groups? For example, trying to use any captured radios or couriers or any other means of communication?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what captured radios you have in mind. I had no such captured radio sets. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you put in place --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let us make a distinction as follows: The radio, if you have the same type of radio in mind that I do, is -- has a bit of a longer range than a -- than an outdated Motorola. As for the couriers that you have in mind, I could only use them in my own area of Jaglici and Brezova Njiva to pass the message across. I did not have a vehicle. I didn't have planes, like the Serbs did. I didn't have shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a reaction to the transcript. The witness said as for the couriers, I could only send a man. He did not really say "I could use them." He stated that he could only send a man to notify them over there, not a courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that correct, Mr. Ademovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, a man. There were no couriers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can simplify this part, Mr. Di Fazio, if you don't mind me interfering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, you've said that when you listened to information over the radio, over the Motorola, which was of interest or which was important to the nearby groups, Jaglici and the other one, that you took it upon yourself to share that information, to pass on that information to those two groups. How did you do it? This is basically what Mr. Di Fazio asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would send out a man who was there nearby. We were all there. I would send Haso or Alija to let the other ones know that they were moving in this direction, that there were ten or 20 or 30 Serb soldiers who -- who were about to attack them, that people should take care. Because behind them there were people doing farm work who could get killed, because there were such instances of people being abducted from their fields and killed. It was in that sense that I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does this help you close this part here or move to the next part, or would you like to pursue it further, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one more matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies to the interpreters. I had my microphone switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one last topic on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, I think your testimony was, you were up in the Rupoglav, which is the highest elevation in your area, you said, looking at the battles that were taking place, and you said that you saw -- and you -- you said that you saw Serb reinforcements arriving in some trucks at one point to assist in some battle or skirmish. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you use your radio to warn fighters of these coming Serb reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I use the Motorola when I was able to see the area with my own eyes? As a professional, I knew what the use of my Motorola meant under the circumstances. It would equal to suicide, because you -- you have to see what sort of technology the Serbs had. They would have located me within 100 metres, and they would have destroyed me. I was only following closely what they were saying. From my vantage point of Rupoglav, if you look at the map, the surrounding terrain is low lying, and with the binoculars that I had, at least one kilometre from Andagina Njiva and from Kravica to Kajici there is this stretch of the road that links Kajici and Jezestica. That was the area that I could see, and why would I be telling somebody else about things that I could see myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but I believe that this is very important. When the witness referred to the Serb technology, he said specifically that they had goniometers, which did not enter into the transcript, and it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, did you mention goniometers, Mr. Ademovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, please, what goniometers are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you this: The most cutting edge technology that could be used at the time for espionage purposes that the Serb forces had were positioned above Ljubovija, in that area, and I knew about this before the outbreak, because this technology was used for monitoring foreign intelligence services and collecting intelligence to that effect. Within the range of 50 kilometres, every conversation taking place on any sort of device could be detected within 50 metres. These were the kind of detectors, goniometers, that they possessed. And I was aware of the existence of this technology and was very careful in using my Motorola. My silence over the Motorola was to save people's lives. I don't know if I've made myself clear. The same type of devices, goniometers, were to be found in the area of Milicko Brdo or Rogac. I believe that yesterday or the day before yesterday in my testimony I mentioned this in passing, but I did not have the chance to expand on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Just about finished up with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you're up there on the -- at the highest elevation in your village and you see the Serb reinforcements arrive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, let him finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you're up there on your high elevation in the village and you see the Serb reinforcements arrive, did you arrange for someone to go and warn the fighters, the Muslim fighters in the area where the reinforcements were, to warn them that the Serbs were sending in reinforcements? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said, from that area both myself and the Jaglici group could see everything. Look at the map. You see it's a large clearing. There a clear view in front. And they would have been able to see it for themselves, so there was no need to go and tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. Did you ever join the 280th Brigade? Did you actually become a member of that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On paper, in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was that the first time you ever became aware that you were supposed to be in army?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never tried to avoid being on the side of the army which was defending its country. I never doubted whether I wanted to join it or not. I always will want that. When -- I was in the group then, and when demilitarisation was finished and when technical issues were being resolved, instructions arrived from Tuzla in 1994, and I was made part of the 280th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these were simply technical issues. There was no military activity at the time because the area had been demilitarised. So there was nothing we could do actively with respect to combat activities, because, of course, I was very happy that this was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So your position is that you were only ever technically a member of the 280th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both de facto and de jure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about being -- about your position as -- or whether or not you held a position as assistant commander for security, and you said that you -- and your reply was - this is 27th of October, page 20: "Allegedly they said I was assistant commander for security and then assistant to the commander for morale, but I was never that. I never seen or saw that." What exactly did you mean by that? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with your interpretation of this text. It might have been misinterpreted. I did not deny that I was an assistant commander on paper in 1994, but I did deny categorically that I was assistant commander for morale, or moral guidance. I would never have performed that duty because it has nothing to do with me, my character, my upbringing, because I feel this is a radically limited area and I am not that type of man. I feel myself to be a bit different. However, as for security, I did say, yes, I was an assistant commander. Let me clarify. Assistant commander for morale, or moral guidance, as it was called, is something that is not in line with my character. It has nothing to do with me. However, as for the post of assistant commander for security, I was that technically in the 280th Brigade, and that is something that does suit my character. However, as for that period, it was the time of demilitarisation so there could be no activities. But they insisted on completing certain things in order for us to be recognised. They said if we didn't do those things, we wouldn't be recognised. So I had to provide proof retroactively of my membership, and I even had to go through certain administrative proceedings because the representatives in Tuzla were very rigorous and very critical in this respect. And I think that I have stated this quite clearly. For every man in my group, I had to personally go through administrative proceedings. And even to this day with respect to the dead or missing, the status of individual men has still not been settled. From 1995, that is. And an injustice has been committed against these people because they were Muslims. Individuals are implementing a certain ideology. I respect you, but unfortunately, I have to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're going to finish today. We're going to finish, there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Registrar, could you pass on this information to Victims and Witnesses. One moment, because I don't want to jump to conclusions. Will there be a re-examination, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So I wonder if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's very likely we'll be able to finish today. Please communicate this information to the VW section. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I wonder if you would be so kind as to break a little earlier. I'd like to rework my cross-examination to make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time. You know how --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's about eight or nine minutes, I think, before. Can we break now and I'll rework it and we'll get to the end of it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. That's the least of the problems. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Do you need more than 25 minutes? If you need 30 minutes, we'll give you 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll play it safe. Let's have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown Exhibit D855.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Ademovic, did you actually see this particular document back in 1994? Did you actually see this particular one? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not, but as I testified previously, I did work on the basis of their instructions and what is contained in this document. As I said, pursuant to this document, I was given a form to fill in. I filled it in with the words "Susnjari unit," as far as I can recall, but this was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And while we're on it -- sorry, Madam Usher, I should have asked you earlier, could the witness be shown D856. And furthermore, P36. Yes, P36.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Firstly, look at P36. That's a form that's apparently completed by Mr. Oric. It's the same type of form, isn't it, as D856. In fact, it's identical, isn't it? It's filled out by someone else, presumably or apparently by Mr. Oric, but it's the same pro forma form or document; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, both --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I haven't seen it properly. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. You agree they're the same form, one apparently filled out by Mr. Oric and the other one which you filled out; correct? Okay?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oric did not fill this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How do you know? I'm talking about P36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, because I can see from here, I see he's holding documents in his right hand and also documents in his left hand. So I want to make sure that we don't have a confusion now. So could you help us, please. Tell us what he's holding. P36.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. You've got --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's apparently completed by Mr. Oric. Just tell me, do you agree that it is apparently, it looks like it on the face, when your eyes go up and down the page and look at the information, it's apparently completed by Mr. Oric. You agree, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, where it says 1, 2, as far as 9, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What's wrong there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look. Look at the handwriting and the letters. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same page. Look at 11. Don't you see a difference there? Look at 16, row 16, then -- isn't there an evident difference in the handwriting? So it wasn't one and the same person who filled this in, all of it. Do you agree with me? Do you see the difference? Have you noticed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is another fake, a forgery, is it? We've just uncovered another one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's an unfair way of characterising it. He's just saying it's a different form of writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. I take the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll approach it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You're saying -- I want to understand you, okay? You're saying there are two different types of handwriting, and what do you -- what are you concluding from that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conclude that Mr. Oric did not fill this in. Look at the difference. I'm talking about the handwriting. I'm neither saying that it is or that it is not a forgery, but that one and the same person did not fill in this entire document, which gives grounds to doubt that it is not valid. And look at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What is at the end of the document that makes you suspicious?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "In Srebrenica, the 10th of January, 1994." And down below I see the year 1993 typed out. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, please. Look at the signature. Look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, what about the signature?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a full stop after the signature, isn't there? After the signature there's a full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the signature, isn't there a full stop there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. And what's -- what's the conclusion therefore? I'm sorry, I'm trying to understand you.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you sign your name or when I sign my name, do you put a full stop at the end? I never put a full stop at the end of my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why I should put a full stop after my signature, and I don't see why Mr. Oric should do that, if he did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you look at the text, there's an evident difference. You can't convince me that this was filled in by one and the same person. I mean, these columns here. I can't say this was filled in by Mr. Oric. You cannot convince me of that. It doesn't mean that he never filled in a similar document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no evidence that he filled in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Just while we're on this particular document, and now that you've raised these issues, do you know if -- just going back to item number 2, do you know if Mr. Oric's father's name is Dzemal?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you happen to know if his mother's maiden name -- the name of his mother and her maiden name was Hata Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Fata but Hata Mustafic. I must say it is Mustafic because she is the sister of my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations about P36, but -- and in fact I'm done with P36 now. But that type of document, including the one that you completed, D856, you sent that back to Tuzla. You sent D856, your particular application, back to Tuzla, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not send it. I only filled it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why didn't you send it?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I send it? I was out on the field. I filled it in in my village, and I don't know who sent it. In my document, underneath, it says 1994. In the case Mr. Oric, it says 1993. It's an evident difference. My document, as far as I can recall, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to -- fine. Okay. I just want to be clear about something. D -- you have D856 in front of you, don't you? You can answer that, I'm sure, with yes --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. That's your form; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Did you --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which I filled in. But it wasn't valid. It was never recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you send it back to Tuzla? Did you get it physically somehow from your location, wherever it was, on your farm or wherever, in the Srebrenica area, from that area to Tuzla? Did you send it to Tuzla, that document D856? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The form I filled in on the ground in my village of Susnjari in 1994 - it says here 1994 - I handed it over to the colleague in Milacevici, and where he took it or how he took it, I didn't go into that. All I know is that I received a negative reply and that what I filled in was never accepted. As I said, I had to provide proof that I was a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they would not recognise the unit in Susnjari the way I filled it in. However, I had to prove this, and fortunately, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And you saw other documents, not just this type of documents but other military documents coming from Tuzla, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever documents I saw, I filled them in, and these are essentially the documents here. If there is another document, please show it to me and then we will discuss it. I'm here for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that it was possible to communicate with Tuzla, send correspondence, documents, to and fro, from Srebrenica to Tuzla, and back? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like a time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to intervene myself precisely on that. What time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Early 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Early 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1994, there was some sort of packet communication on the basis of which we received the packet by Mr. Sadic, and we worked on the basis of that. It was physically impossible to communicate because we were too far. However, this arrived in my place in Susnjari, this particular document, and then I personally filled it in. It bears my signature. It is evident, because I recognise it. But without -- of course, it's without the full stop at the end. Unfortunately, this was never recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So the packet communication system facilitated you sending or people sending documents from Srebrenica to Tuzla and back, in early 1994 at least; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was when the packet communication functioned, in 1994 and 1995, when I was definitely put on paper technically as the assistant commander for security. There are documents to that effect, and I cannot now claim that this is contrary to what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And how about 1993? Was it possible to send documents to and fro using this packet system of communication?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that I wrote letters that the UNHCR or, rather, the Red Cross sent my family. Now, by what means this was sent, I don't know. It was all censored. I wrote letters to my children. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wrote back. Whenever I received correspondence, the Serbian side censored it and I never knew what was written beneath the black marker. Unfortunately, this was also the case. Therefore, my right of speech was denied in my correspondence with my children. I wasn't entitled to express my sentiments. I can bring you hundreds of documents of that kind that I still keep where I was communicating with my children. Doesn't this amount to terror, to ultimate censorship of what is usually normal in a civilised society?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand your concerns. Do I take it, therefore, that private correspondence, albeit censored, was possible in 1993 from between Srebrenica and Tuzla? After demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was taken care of from the Serbian side in Bratunac. I think you are very familiar with these matters. I think we should move on. I could speak for five days about my experience, things that I went through. My own child sent me a letter three years later to see if I was still alive. Was there really a need for it to be controlled and censored? Do you consider that to be normal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it from your -- just to close this issue of communications and correspondence, I take it that you just can't tell this Trial Chamber whether or not there was a packet communication system operating in 1993 that facilitated the transfer of documents such as D856 between the Srebrenica area and Tuzla? You just don't know. There might have been or there might not have been. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I'm sure of is the year 1994. The period prior to that is something I cannot vouch for. I told you that in May 1993, I was going through a very difficult period. My health was very poor, and I apologise, Your Honours, but I believe that there is evidence to show that I was ill. I was at my parents' home, undergoing a treatment, and I would be speculating. However, I am definitely certain about the year 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw -- I saw you standing up and then sitting down again, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the witness had clearly answered. He said that was when the packet communication functioned, in 1994 and 1995. Mr. Di Fazio was saying, "I take it from your answer that there's a possibility that it worked in 1993." The witness never allowed for that possibility and his evidence has only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions on this document, that's all. Entry number 40 of D846 -- I do apologise to Madam Usher for not informing her that the document should stay there. 856. The same one. The request for admittance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Items number 40 and 41, okay? Entry 40 and 41. There are two questions in paragraphs 40 and 41. The date of putting yourself at the disposal of the RBiH armed forces and the date of your deployment in the RBiH army, and in both questions you answered 18th of April, 1992, as being the date of putting yourself at disposal and date of deployment. Why did you answer in that way?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the 18th of April, 1992, I made myself available, placed myself at disposal, and I personally thought that this date should also be recognised as valid. However, as my papers arrived into Vlah containing this entry, the Susnjari unit, I received a response as contained in the document by Mr. Sadic and dated 1994, who cautioned us about the inadmissibility of what we had written. I stood by what I had written before, and when I arrived in Tuzla, I had to retroactively, through administrative proceedings, prove the validity of what was contained in this document. When again they refused to recognise this, I went back to the job that I'm still doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. But your evidence to this Trial Chamber has been that in 1992, you were a member of a local grouping. You were a member of a local grouping, a local group of fighters with no command structure. You couldn't enforce orders. There was no command structure amongst the groups. How did you consider yourself to be a member of the RBiH army in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I partially executed the order. In the technical sense, I put it on paper, but again I did not fully accept their order. I did not fully accept their order. At a later stage, when I retroactively wanted to obtain my rights through administrative proceedings, I simply abandoned the whole matter, and I would never again in my life wish to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance on this document. I'd like to ask you some questions about some of the other documents that were shown to you by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Usher I'll be asking that D845 and 846 be produced to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Ademovic, appears to be a confidential document prepared by the Serb military. You were shown it and asked questions about it by Madam Vidovic. The second part of the document deals with a report. And in the English, Your Honours, it's the ERN ending 67. Do you have the second part of the document dealing with report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, I think we need to move the report. No, no. You just -- that's it. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Which part of this page do you want us to concentrate on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's on page 67 in the English translation, and it's the topic Defence, the small -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the Serbs are saying in this confidential document: "While conducting combat activities, units - Serb units - do not make adequate shelters and rarely set minefields," and it goes on to talk about problems the causes, and then they say this: "A small, organised enemy group is able to make defence units move and run away ..." Were you able to have that effect on the Serb forces when you were operating with your group? Did you ever see the effectiveness of small, organised groups on --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which paragraph are you referring to? Is it document 967, which I have? Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's under the heading "Defence" and -- "Defence." Do you see the word "Defence"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the last sentence: "A small, organised enemy group is able to make defence units move and run away (Kalesija-Brezik)." Do you see that? And the document, they seem to be talking generally. All right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you agree with the Serb -- the Serbs' assessment about themselves, that they were -- small, organised enemy groups were having some impact, at least, by making defence units move and run away? Did you ever see, observe that yourself?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this portion refers to Kalesija. Do you know where Kalesija is? It physically abuts Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that. Did you ever observe similar, similar phenomena in your area; small, organised enemy groups able to make defence units move and run away? Did you see it or not? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're about to confuse him the way you put the question, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm going to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm going to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just forget about this part. Let's go to paragraph 7. Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. The question has been withdrawn. Let's move to something else now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one more topic on this document, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you have paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see it at the page ending 668.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Paragraph 8. "Morale Amongst Fighters - Evaluation, Improvement Measures." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Serbs seem to say this in their confidential document: "Morale is very low. What can one say about the morale of fighters when they do not want to defend their own homes and abandon them? Fighters from burned-down villages who stayed in this territory are rare." Now, do you know what burned-downed villages the Serbs might be referring to in this confidential military document? Have you got any idea?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they had in mind, but over at my turf, Jaglici, Brezova Njiva, Susnjari, I did not torch a single village. I don't know that there were any torched villages. And now they could have on their part named the villages that they had in mind. As I earlier said, I filled in the form with the entries that are there, and I did not -- or, rather, I do not hesitate to say publicly they should be the ones to admit which villages they had in mind. I am convinced that this is mere propaganda, something that does not reflect or, rather, deliberately, erroneously reflects the situation, because in my area of Birac I never experienced such a situation. Quite the contrary. Their morale was quite high. They were really intent on destroying us. I invite you to come over to my area. I returned there and I'm still alive, and you will be -- we will receive you as a precious guest. You will see where I was and where I was active. And this invitation applies not only to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And just to wrap up this topic, you never saw any -- I'll withdraw that. In -- in 1992 and 1993, you never received any information or saw for yourself the deliberate burning and torching of Serb villages by Muslim forces at all. That's something you -- that you never heard of or saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area where I was active in 1992, not a single house was torched by the Muslims. And this refers to the area where I was. I only told you that on the 8th of August, 1992, when we were under a fierce attack from Djermani and Jezestica, the men from the 16th Muslim, under the leadership of Rizvanovic, they acted and then things happened that we know of. However, they did not set those facilities on fire, rather, the fire was a result of the shelling. At least I speak for what I saw. Otherwise, I would be speculating. There are neighbours in Lipenovici and Vratinci and the area where I even perhaps had the opportunity of making an incursion and attacking them. I chose not to. We are still good neighbours and friends. We still have coffee together today. Perhaps you won't believe me, but that's the accurate situation on the ground. When I came before this institution, I met a neighbour who I was able to drink coffee with and have a chat, and I will tell you that the houses of my neighbours, some of them are still intact while mine is destroyed. You should look into that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you have a relative called Sead -- Sead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know why but there are many errors on the transcript today. The witness said that the neighbouring houses were all intact, whereas the transcript reads some of them are still intact, and these were Serbian houses that were destroyed. And "my house was destroyed," that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Sead, Sead Ademovic?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Seads. One is the son of Ramo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the other?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the other is the son of Alija. They were born in the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And from your area, from your village perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ademovics were in my village and then in the village of Gologvina [phoen]. There are Ademovics in three or four municipalities in the Drina area. There are Ademovics in Sarajevo as well, and if you want, you can check it up and see how many there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do either of the two Ademovics that you mentioned, the son of -- the two Ademovics that you mentioned named Sead, did they ever operate in the military police, in any military police formation?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which period of time you're referring to when you talk about the active military police. Is it the course of 1992? But I need a date. What do you have in mind?
