Because in the course of 1992, I never left my area. If you're referring to the active military police, then this could not have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll show you some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And Madam Usher is getting her exercise today, and I apologise for this, but P40 and P41, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And while that document -- and while that document's -- sorry. Your Honour, there's -- I think there's a problem, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have P40 and P41 on the list or, rather, we don't have P40 on the list. We would like to see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P41 was on the list, and P40, too. I agree with you that I don't see P40 myself either, unless there is a revised -- which there was this morning, I didn't bring it with me. But I think that one which was revised referred to P441 and P441.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I agree. It's probably not on your list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think she's objecting to the use of this document. She just wants to, obviously, have access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, yes. Yes, please, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to look at the documents to see what their contents are. I mean the P40 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're three-liners, four-liner documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can put them on the ELMO or we can use the Sanction if it's available on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Whatever is simplest and fastest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the simplest and fastest, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're essentially the same type of document, if Your Honours please. Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can look at these two documents at the same time, I think, for -- to save time. It won't take long to read them. They're very short. Okay? And it talks about a patrol group consisting of two fellows, Midhat Zukic from Potocari, and a gentleman named Sead Ademovic, carrying out various duties. That's in P40. The same two fellows appear in P41, and both documents are dated the 19th of December, 1992. And P41 also refers to those two fellows carrying out various duties. Now, now we've got a date that I'm interested in, December 1992. Did either of the two Sead Ademovics that you know carry out military police duties in December of 1992? Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear sir, on the 19th of December, 1992, on that day the ground was aflame in Susnjari. There were thousands of refugees on the run. What sort of insinuations are these? I have already stated Ademovic Sead son of Ramo and Ademovic Sead son of Alija. Is this physically possible or, rather, was it physically possible under the circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I really don't want to trouble you a lot with these documents. It's a simple question. Having seen the documents and the content, my question is this: Did either of the Sead Ademovics that you know, did they perform duties in December 1992 in any type of military police organisation? If you don't know, say so. If you -- if that did not happen, tell us; and if it did happen, tell us that as well, okay? I just want to know.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I have to clarify this. You refuse to understand me. You don't want to follow the situation as I described it, the situation I myself was in and all those people up there on the 19th of December. Please look at the stamp. I refer you again to the stamp. Can you convince me that this is an original document? This is pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And just to finally wrap it up, are both documents pure fabrications or just one of them?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Just look at the difference between these two documents. Look at the way the stamp is used. You're an educated man. You know what stamps are used for and in what manner. Please don't misunderstand me, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, I think we're making reasonable progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you first came here to testify, you briefly described village guards, and Madam Vidovic was asking you questions, page 26. She was showing you a document, and you gave -- and you gave an answer and said this: "The village guards are something completely different. They consist of smaller disorganised groups that are not coordinated with others. They are not well equipped, and they possibly have some sports or hunting weapons." And then you went on to describe what was in the document by saying: "Whereas here we clearly deal with a well organised, well equipped, well coordinated units, both locally and in the general area which form part of the system, and I repeat, the system." Now, it's your definition of village guards that I'm interested in. You're quite clear about them, aren't you? They have to be small. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They're disorganised. They're not coordinated. They're not well equipped, and they don't have military -- military weaponry. They've got sports or hunting weapons. How did you come to that definition of village guard? Why do you say that that's what makes up a village guard?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's what it was like in practice. I don't exclude the possibility of there being one disorganised group of three or four men with a weapon that is not a sports weapon or a hunting weapon, but there's a lack of equipment, and I think you understand what the equipment and materiel of an organised unit linked up to a system should be. So these are two quite different concepts. The man in a village guard has two, three, or five bullets, or one round, while a member of a well-organised group that is linked up in a system has logistics both in the field and in the rear. In the rear, he has logistics in depots. He has artillery support; 60, 80, 120-millimetre mortars, tanks, multiple rocket launchers and so on and so forth. Another thing, a village guard is near its village, whereas organised units are linked up and go to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We can move on really fast from this. Did you ever see any village guards, the type you understand to be village regards, operating in Serb villages? Were you ever aware of the presence of the sort of village guard that you had in mind when you gave your definition?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I have been quite clear. Working as a police officer, I went to various areas in the Srebrenica municipality, and I saw something like that throughout Srebrenica municipality, both in Serb villages and in Muslim villages in March, April, up to the 18th of April when I definitely made myself available. However, the information I received from the ground and in the operations centre was sufficient for me to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know if the Serbs kept those village guards after April of 1992? The ones operating in their villages, I mean.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In certain areas and certain villages, they had already organised themselves well and linked up into a system of the army of Republika Srpska. They had also linked up to the JNA. And they were joined by units, as I said. They were supplied with equipment and materiel by units withdrawing from Croatia. I think it's quite clear to this Court, so I do apologise for saying this, but it's absurd to ask me such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P84.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: While that document is being prepared, do you know a place called the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a well-known health resort, and I invite you to be my guest there. Not just you yourself but others. It's a well-known health resort. I see you're smiling. It has a century's-long tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I could use it, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I invite you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I believe that even Mr. Wubben would be prepared to join you. The thing is I don't know whether we're talking of the same thing. And your question was the Domavija hotel, and the witness is referring to the Domavija resort, which I think are not exactly the same thing. And the Domavija hotel that you referred to in your question, I take it, is the Domavija hotel in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Domavija resort that he's referring to may not necessarily be in Srebrenica. So I think -- let the witness explain. We are talking about the Domavija hotel in Srebrenica, which we saw and which doesn't look like much a Domavija spa resort or health resort any more, if it ever was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building called Domavija is a hotel which is part of the Guber Banja spa system, which is where I was inviting this gentleman to be my guest, really my guest. And this is in the immediate vicinity, some 300 metres away from Argentarija, another building within this hotel complex where they had warm baths, saunas, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to the Domavija hotel building in Srebrenica, which I suppose you know about. So your question, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, Madam Usher, I want to look at portion of the P84 that has ERN number ending in 131. This is a handwritten document, if Your Honours please. And in the English, if Your Honours please, it's at page 61. Now, you should have in handwriting there, and it's -- an indication that it appears to be minutes of a staff meeting held on the 8th of July, 1993, at the Domavija hotel, starting at about 11.00. And it says that a number of people attended the meeting, including Mr. Oric, various other personalities, and your name appears there, Sidik Ademovic. Did you ever attend a meeting at the Domavija hotel on the 8th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the document I have here I see has been extracted from its context. I don't want to deny I was there. As far as I can recall, I was, but this document is incomplete. I don't know what this is about. Does this document have an end? Is this a complete document? Is there more material accompanying this document? Give me the entire document if you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. I mean, just confirm or deny your presence at the Domavija hotel for a meeting, I think of the Srebrenica OS staff, on the 8th of July, 1993, which you seem to confirm from -- at least, you're not denying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, this is the time of demilitarisation. There was demilitarisation. I don't see that there was a staff there, but I don't deny attending a meeting, but a staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is demilitarisation. There was no staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I understand. I understand what you're saying. Now, look, you don't have to worry about what the document says. You've told us independently of what the document says that you did go to a meeting in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not denying. He's not saying that he did. He's not denying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll have to go a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you go to a meeting on the 8th of July, 1993, at the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any meeting now you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Any meeting at the Domavija hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the problem, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is confusing for the witness. What the witness testified to earlier was that he attended a meeting in November. I remember that well. But saying that he had been there in July, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already testified that he doesn't deny having been to a meeting on the 8th of July now, but he denies or he finds it strange that it could be as Srebrenica staff or OS staff meeting. Now he's being asked a different question. Does he recall ever having been to a meeting, having attended a meeting in the Domavija hotel in -- on the 8th of July, 1993. Any kind of meeting, not necessarily of the Srebrenica OS staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not attend a meeting of the Srebrenica staff. I did attend a meeting in the Domavija hotel. I seem to remember it was on the 24th of November, yes, but I know that this was a time of demilitarisation and there was no staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. I just want to be clear about it, that's all. So what you're saying is, "No, 8th of July, 1993, I was not at any meeting at the Domavija hotel." That's your position pure and simple; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't remember attending a meeting on this date here, and I don't remember there being a staff. This was a time when there was demilitarisation. At that time, my health was not so good. I was still recuperating. I do not deny attending a meeting in 1993. It was one meeting, probably in October or November. I think it was November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what was that meeting in October or November of 1993 at the Domavija hotel? What was that meeting about and who attended?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the issue discussed was the condition of the refugees and the events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was Mr. Oric at that meeting in October --

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon? I don't think he was, but I could be wrong. It's a long time period. But as far as I can recall, I was quite lost at that meeting. Nothing was clear to me, if I'm not wrong. To the best of my recollection. A long time has elapsed since then. Perhaps I said something at that meeting, a single sentence, or maybe not, but I don't even remember what the meeting was about. Is anything I said reflected in the minutes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. One last issue on this document, Madam Usher, and Mr. Ademovic. I'd like you to look at ERN -- the page with the ERN number ending 156. If Your Honours please, page 71 of the English.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't read out to me what I said if I attended that meeting in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it, Mr. Ademovic. Please answer the questions. You're not here to say whatever comes to your mind. You're asked -- being asked questions, and stick to answering those questions. Yes. We have that page on the Sanction now, on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to. I know it's stressful being here, sitting, answering questions for four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. It's just another similar type of inquiry on my part. Here you have 15th of December, 1993, and it says present at the meeting and it goes through various people, and it says here that -- yes. It says that Mr. Oric is present, and it also appears to have your name there, Sidik Ademovic. Now, again, it's the same sort of question: Did you in fact attend a meeting with these people, the people who are mentioned there, on or about the 15th of December -- or on the 15th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither deny nor confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Madam Usher, I'm done with that document. Mr. Ademovic, do you want to hand it back to the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm letting him have a further look at it. Maybe it possibly makes him remember more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I didn't interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to deprive the witness of the chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why we did not interfere, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ademovic. Do you want to keep looking?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you want to keep looking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to have a further look at that document or are you finished with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for me to look at it any more. As I said, I can neither confirm nor deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it possible that you attended meetings throughout 1993, meetings at which Mr. Oric was present, throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall one or perhaps two meetings. To the best of my recollection, the issues discussed were technical and had to do with the situation on the ground as regards the refugees in every area; the number of refugees, their health, food, and so on. But as far as I can recall, I was often late for these meetings, and I often left early because the area I was coming from was far away. I would leave because these meetings were confused. Things were vague. Nobody knew what the meetings were about, why they had been called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If Your Honours please, I'm just approaching the end, but I can't finish it that quickly. I wonder -- I know it's only five past 12.00. I wonder if you would be prepared to break now. I guarantee that we will finish today and there will be ample time for the Defence for re-examination or any questions on the part of Your Honours. I've really basically got two more topics which I think I can deal with in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is certainly no problem if there is no problem with the Defence. So we will break now. If we break for 30 minutes, that will leave us ample time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. There's no question. We will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to turn and very briefly look at the events on the 8th of August, 1992, which included fighting around Jezestica. You -- on that day you were at the highest point of elevation at the small village of Lupoglava; is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lupoglava is not a village. Jaglici is a village. I believe it's the elevation point 654 or 456. In any case, it is above the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you for that clarification. And that gave you a good view around the area so you could see everything; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, according to the map, I had full control all the way along the Bratunac-Kravica road, the forking off towards Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you had with you on that day your Motorola.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What time did you go up to this high elevation, this high point at Lupoglava?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hardly left this elevation point because the intensity of the attack and the shelling never subsided in that period. On that morning, during that night, and the entire day until the afternoon, I spent my time at that point. So from the -- during the night from the early morning hours. I said I was there on the 6th and the 7th when there was the massacre against the column of people in the direction of Hajducko Groblje. Those were refugees. Throughout this period I was in -- at that particular point observing what was going on. Such were the circumstances. They dictated my whereabouts. It was actually dictated by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why did you stay there on the 8th, the 8th of August? Was there any particular reason that caused you to remain there on the 8th of August at this high elevation with your Motorola?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there with my Motorola because the highest intensity of the infantry attack from Jezestica and Djermani was such that they wanted to capture this elevation point. Some 100 to 150 metres further down, there is a village there in the valley, and in order for this elevation to be -- or, rather, if one captured this elevation point, one could control the entire area. Large numbers of refugees would then be exposed to the risk of being massacred. I had the following choice: To stay alive or die. Luckily, I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you up there with your group of men from Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the left of that particular site, according to the map - that would mean to the east - my group was deployed in the direction of Ravni Buljim, and since this is where the epicenter of the attack was, I wanted to be there in person. To my right, along the Rupoglav axis, along that edge, that part was covered by the lads from the Jaglici group. Further down --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How do you know that was covered by the Jaglici group? Did you speak with them, arrange it beforehand, or not?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They held the area. This area is -- overlooks their village. They followed what was going on clearly, because in front of us there are some clearings and forests. In Djermani, there are meadows. In Stara Jasikovaca, some 200, 300 and 400 metres away from Stara Jagoda were meadows, and you were able to follow what was going on. Just look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear, on that particular day, on the 8th of August, 1992, your group participated in active fighting, as did the Jaglici group, and you cooperated with one another; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had we not helped each other, we would have definitely been defeated by the Serb forces, massacred and destroyed as early as on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in evidence when answering questions from Madam Vidovic, you said that -- you were asked this question and gave this answer: "Apart from Ejub Golic's group and Nurif's unit, were you aware of some other Muslim groups participating in the fighting around Jezestica?" And you answered: "No." What I want to know is this: Did you mean by that that as far as the immediate area around Jezestica, the immediate area around Jezestica, it was only Ejub Golic and Nurif Rizvanovic fighting, but you also were fighting in the area that you've described in your testimony; you and the group from Jaglici. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the defence, and I believe this is clearly stated in my statement. I was along the defence line, and when I was attacked, of course I took part in defensive action. This was not an offensive action on my part. It was defensive. You should draw that distinction. In my area, the Serb forces intensified their infantry supported by artillery from all directions, but from the direction of Djermani, Jezestica, Kajici, and Brezik, and especially from the Rogac plateau. And on my flank the attack was from Lipenovci. I don't want to repeat this, but the infantry intensified their attack, and this is what is stated in my testimony, that I forced to defend myself. And this goes for the Jaglici group and the Brezova Njiva group, as there was an attack also coming from the direction of Bukova Glava and Dubovi. That was the area where I took an active part, but I took an active part in defence. I believe that the attack and the defence are two distinct terms. I believe Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you know that. In subsequent developments, around noon, as I was listening in over my Motorola to the Serbian forces, I learnt that something similar was also going on in Veresinje from the direction of Cizmici, where Golic's men were mentioned. I believe that's what the transcript shows. And in the area of Hajducko Groblje and Siljkovici, this was in front of my area, and I was able to hear and know what was going on. It wasn't impossible to see and hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had no idea that there was going to be fighting -- sorry, that Nurif Rizvanovic and Ejub Golic's men were going to go into action on that particular day? Do I understand that correctly? You didn't know?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had and I obtained, I knew that the Serbian side was about to attack me. When the infantry attack against me started, then the artillery from the direction of Veresinje and Cizmici also opened fire. After these attacks - I believed so at the time but this was confirmed to me later on - Golic simply decided to retreat because they had many -- or, rather, no. Golic decided to push them back because they had many wounded and massacred, and he decided to push them back. Now, as for what was going on in Konjevic Polje, Lolici and Kamenica, where Nurif's unit was stationed, it was only at a later stage that I found out what was going on, and I wish to thank them for having helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So I take it your answer is no, you had no idea that Nurif Rizvanovic was going to go into action that day and operate around Jezestica and you had no idea that Ejub Golic's unit was going to go into action around Jezestica that day. You only found that out afterwards. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made that quite clear. I did not have any official information about him arriving down there, Golic. It was only later on that I learnt about how they arrived over there, where they got their equipment from, and so on. And as I said, I wish to thank them again, because without them, I would not have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree or would you agree with me that it would have made good sense for Ejub Golic and Nurif Rizvanovic to try and let you and your men know what they were going to do and vice versa, since you were all fighting in a fairly close area or area that's relatively close?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they would even try to attempt to let me know about it. I was physically cut off. I told you that the means of communications did not exist. I was only able to follow over my communications device what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You described -- you described of the visit, I think, by Mr. Rizvanovic after fighting had subsided on that day. He came and you saw him on the 8th of August. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness never stated so that he had seen Nurif Rizvanovic and that he had toured the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but before you do: Mr. Di Fazio, what's your comment on Madam Vidovic's remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Wednesday the 26th of October, if Your Honours please, page 53, the -- the witness described fighting subsiding in the late afternoon hours. Page 52. And some men arrived wearing uniforms. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But really, I don't have the transcript here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am relying on what you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm just giving you -- and then I'll get to the crunch. That was the preface to the comments. And there was talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I want you to read where he states that Mr. Rizvanovic arrived and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "Did you know Mr. Nurif Rizvanovic from before?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him well from before the war. He was a military man. He was quite a controversial figure, but everything that I knew about him then was before the war, from the workplace where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you talk with Hodzic Safet and Dzemo Tihic and Nurif Rizvanovic about the events in August 1992, and what did they tell you?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "A. They told me that in early August they arrived in the Konjevic Polje area and that on that day they were in the area of Lolici and the nearby village of Kamenica. Through their communications devices they had -- they had heard that the Serbian side wanted to seize the area of Jaglici and Susnjari, Lupoglava, and Ravni Buljim." So I might have misunderstand. The witness wanted to talk about subsequent conversations and Madam Vidovic may be quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I allowed Madam Vidovic to intervene and stopped the witness and asked you to go to the transcript because I was sure Madam Vidovic was right. You don't need to go through this. Please wait until the next question and answer the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Anyway, did you see any men from Nurif Rizvanovic's unit on that day, on the 8th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, please do not put names into my mouth. Nurif Rizvanovic never came to me. That is not what the transcript states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said stop. I told you forget what you had heard before and answer the next question. And the next question does not deal with Rizvanovic himself. It deals with his men, whether you saw those men on the 8th of August. Please answer that question and forget the rest. Otherwise, you'll be here -- we're trying our best to send you home tomorrow. If you're not going to cooperate, you're going to end up here until Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the question is: Did you see any gentlemen from Nurif Rizvanovic's unit late in that day?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came to me, Safet Hodzic, Hakija Malic, and Ahmo Tihic's brother Dzemo Tihic, son of Mujo, from Skelani. Do you need any further information?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. Thank you, Mr. Ademovic. That's good. Did they tell what you they had known about Serb intentions prior to the 8th of August? Serb intentions in relation to that area, what they were planning on doing.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated in evidence that they told me that they were in the locality of Lolici and the hamlet of Kamenica - Topuska Kamenica, because there is another Kamenica in Zvornik - and that they had all the necessary means of communication and they were able to follow what was going on, and that the Serbian forces along the axis towards Lupoglava had the intention of seizing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's exactly right. That's what I'm asking you about, you see. So they came and told you, didn't they, that they knew what the Serbs were up to. They hadn't told you about that, had they? They didn't tell you that the Serbs were going to attack and try and seize the area of Jaglici, your very own village Susnjari, Lupoglava, and Ravni Buljim. They hadn't informed of you this crucial information, had they? You might have known about it, but they hadn't told you about it.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it, but they were not able to inform me about it. I was physically separated from them. Another thing: They did not know that I had a communications device, because I did not know that they were in the area. They found out about what was going on through their communications device and then acted further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said also that, in answer to a question from Madam Vidovic, that no Suceska unit could have participated in this fighting on the 8th of August in your area. Why precisely is that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the map and you will see that I was encircled, and look at what the distance was across the rugged terrain. I believe it is of some 15 kilometres as the crow flies, although I'm not an expert. I believe it was practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So even if the -- even if the Muslim forces had been able to plan any operations in the area of Jezestica on the 8th of August, 1992, and think ahead, plan for it, your position is that it would have been impossible for the Suceska unit to participate. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in any sense including the practical one. They were unable to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And just as far as events -- you were asked some questions about events in Kravica in early January of 1992 -- 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 1993. 1993. If I suggested to you that that was a planned attack, a dawn attack by Muslim forces on the village, would you agree with that proposition or not?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just -- last topic, very, very last topic, I promise you, Mr. Ademovic. I just want to show you some footage of a speech given by Mr. Oric, and I'd like you to listen to it. Just have a listen to it and then I'll ask you something about it. Can the witness be shown the video clip P441, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you hear? Good.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I'm especially honoured today to present a programme of the festive academy marking the second anniversary of the Srebrenica Armed Forces Staff, which nowadays bears the name of the command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica, and is in the structure of the 2nd Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On behalf of the command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica, the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica, the cultural centre and the cultural club Srebrenica, I call upon the commander of the 8th Operations Group, Mr. Naser Oric. "Naser Oric: Before I begin, I want to greet everyone present and congratulate all soldiers and people on Kurban-Bajram. "Dear guests, officers and soldiers, we have gathered here today to mark the day when the staff of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence was founded, the staff that developed into a command body of the Srebrenica armed forces and the formation and the command of the 8th Operations Group of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the structure of the 2nd Corps. Such gatherings are always an opportunity to recall the very beginning of the war. Precisely 25 months ago these people in Eastern Bosnia fell into a trap of unilateral fascist wave, poisoned with nationalistic ineradicable barbarism in the centre of Europe, a story that has lasted 25 months so far and I do not know how long of -- the Muslim-Bosniak people cannot be told at one such gathering. I hope this time without demagogic approaches, but I must remind you that two years ago on today's date the staff of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence was founded. Then the municipal and party politicians. The bare-handed Muslim people entered a defence war unrecorded in history. Self-organised, the first battles began on the 20th of April, 1992 in Potocari, followed by the defence of Suceska on the 1st and 2nd of May, 1992, the combat in the town of Srebrenica on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of May, a sabotage on the 7th of May, 1992 in Potoci near Osmace. The first combat actions in Vidikovac on the 8th of May 1992 and the 15th of May in 1992. Commanding officers of self-organised units met on today's date two years ago in Bajramovic and established the Joint Command of the entire -- the Srebrenica staff. I will not bother you today with all the tasks and decisions performed by the staff in the past period. I shall just mention that the staff members had to perform for us duties ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Firstly, do you -- do you -- are you aware of any of the military structures that Mr. Oric is apparently referring to; the staff of the Srebrenica TO, the command body of the Srebrenica armed forces, the 8th Operational Group? Are you aware of the existence, the actual real existence of such bodies?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know of the existence according to the directives. We worked upon the first document of Mr. Sadic and that these were technical issues and administrative matters, as I have previously stated. Everything else was just groups and group leaders. And as far as I can see, this is the point in time when commander Naser Oric was appointed from Tuzla. I don't know who appointed him. He was not my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And last question: Would you agree with me, Mr. Ademovic, that Mr. Naser Oric is a man who is extremely well placed to comment upon the formation of armed groupings in the Srebrenica area? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know who from Tuzla appointed him. I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- but that's not -- I'm not asking about Tuzla and who appointed who. I'm just asking you this: You agree with me, don't you, that Mr. Naser Oric, he's a man who knows a lot about the formation of armed groupings in the Srebrenica area, the formation of any military groupings and how they developed. Don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he had information. He could only have had information about his own village, Potocari. I probably had more information than he did because I had three groups in my immediate vicinity, and afterwards I had Babuljice, Lehovici, and so on. He could only know about Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering my questions, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Di Fazio. Madam Vidovic, is there re-examination? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ademovic, you saw this video clip shown to you by the Prosecutor which was taken when the alleged commemoration was taking place.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe that Mr. Oric was reading from a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was reading something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that he was holding a piece of paper in his hands while speaking?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Before the demilitarisation, did you spend any time at all in Srebrenica apart from that one occasion you described in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm the date. Around the 24th of November, 1992, when I was asking for assistance, and I think around January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1993? I'm asking you about before the demilitarisation. Apart from that meeting or encounter you described with somebody in Srebrenica, did you go to any other meetings in Srebrenica, and were you familiar with the situation in Srebrenica throughout 1992 until demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assert with full confidence: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other contacts apart from the ones you described?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't have had, and I did say that in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ademovic, I will ask you now to look again at documents P40, P41 and P269.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have a question connected to all three documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While the documents are being distributed, I'll ask you the following: Is it correct that Bosnia and Herzegovina, before the war, was part of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a legally recognised republic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And was the socialist system in place there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that socialist system, you were a policeman. Do you recall whether the use of stamps was regulated and prescribed in detail?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is pursuant to international rules, not just local rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, Mr. Ademovic, whether this was strictly regulated in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to better understand your testimony, on more than one occasion you told the Court today and asked the Prosecutor to look at the stamps on documents. I will ask you to look at all three of these documents in the place where the stamp is, and then I'll ask you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I only have two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, he is saying that he has only got two documents, and Madam Vidovic wants him to refer to three documents. So the third one has arrived. What I suggest that we do is that we also see these -- if they are available on Sanction, I think it would be much easier. These are Prosecution exhibits. Because all we need to see is the stamp, actually. Otherwise, Madam Usher can put the page on which the stamp is affixed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, there has to be -- we have to log back on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put them on the ELMO and the witness can see them on the monitor himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, can you put those parts of all three documents where the stamp is on the ELMO, or first you can put P40 and P41, and then we can look at P269 if you can't put all three on at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please. In the former Yugoslavia, in practice, was a stamp ever placed on top of a signature? Did you ever see this as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the rule that a signature had to be clearly visible and so did the stamp used?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The stamp had to be separate from the signature. If there was no "MP" there, then the stamp could cover only the first letter of the signature, possibly the first two letters. But I can say that using a stamp on top of a signature is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was never done on official documents in practice?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, according to the rules when forging.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please look at the third document. Mr. Ademovic, your answer is not clear in the record. I asked you whether you agreed that in official documents in practice a stamp was never put on top of the signature. What was your reply?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was never put on top of a signature. And then I clarified this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, look at the third document. When you were explaining this document, is this what you were trying to tell Their Honours, that the stamp is covering the signature?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as in the previous document. This is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from this being wrong, Mr. Ademovic, I want to ask you the following: In your life, did you ever have an opportunity to see Naser Oric's signature?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that signature, did it look like this? Is this the signature, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I see now with the stamp placed there wrongly, I can assert with full liability no. And the printed name beneath that is inappropriate. And there's not just one signature here, as far as I can see. There's another one here below the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in connection with this document, look at the first page of this document P269. It says: "After the action on the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "-- carried out in Potocari where a number of Arkan's men were killed and Arkan himself wounded and later succumbed to his injuries." Have you seen this, "Arkan himself wounded and later succumbed to his injuries"? Please, did you ever get the information that Arkan was wounded in this area and especially that he succumbed to his injuries?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything like that. I would have been very happy if that had happened on that day. This world would be a much more peaceful place had this been so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Arkan was killed?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed by his own men in Belgrade, the men who prepared him to be the way he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did this kind of information go round Srebrenica and Potocari in May while you were still able to move around there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assert that the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you briefly something about your Motorola. The Prosecutor asked you how you sent information to neighbouring groups, and you said -- when there was a Serb attack, and you said you would send somebody who was in the vicinity, or Alija, to tell them. Did you use particular men every time or were the names you mentioned only an example?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These names were used at random. It was different people. I said Huso. It could have been Murat. It could have been Osman. It could have been Omer. It could have been my next-door neighbour Markovic, Dusko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you whether or not you were only technically a member of the 270th Brigade [as interpreted], and you replied that it was your position that you were only technically a member of the 280th Brigade. At least, that's what the record states. And your answer was: "De facto and de jure." My question is: Were you a member of that brigade de facto, or was it only on paper?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "De facto and de jure," what I meant to say was technically only on paper, and that's what I said in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you meant only on paper.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant technically, only on paper, and I think I clarified this sufficiently. I explained how I was put there, because I participated in making the list of those men. I didn't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any questions? Do you have any questions? We don't have any further questions for you, Mr. Ademovic, which basically means that you're free to go back home. But before you leave this courtroom, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on my own behalf and on behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence at this trial as one of the Defence witnesses. You will very soon leave this courtroom and you will receive all the assistance you require from our staff to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. Before you leave, I also wish you a safe journey back home on behalf of everyone here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I wish to thank the Presiding Judge especially, the ladies and the gentlemen from the Defence, and also the gentlemen from the Prosecutor's office, and my -- Mr. Oric, and all those who participated in the proceedings during my testimony. I hope I will be of assistance and that my testimony will help establish the truth. It was not my intention to defend anyone here but simply to tell the truth. Once again, thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I understand, Mr. Wubben, that you wanted to raise a matter. No, no. It's -- you have got 20 minutes in which to do so, and I hope you won't take as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be brief. It is a matter of seeking guidance from Your Honours as it pertains to the decision by yesterday, and we are working on the disclosure -- the disclosures and organising as such. We find out about the orders Your Honours gave, and a part of it raised -- rose two questions. It's the -- it's the fifth page, in which, and I quote Your Honours' orders: "The Prosecution to conduct a thorough and complete search for Rule 68 material." With a view to that order, the question raised whether or not is meant to be for the Prosecution to start from scratch again a search for Rule 68 material, as we are already doing for years upon our own initiatives, upon new material, and upon request by the Defence giving us search terms do already those searches, or that the accent of that order is within the declaration that is requested, stating what searches have been made, et cetera, and giving details about that. So is the accent a request, an order to conduct a new search from scratch, totally new, or is it that we should provide the Trial Chamber a statement giving a complete overview what searches has been done, including the new searches as raised and discussed in the past week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's number one. Perhaps we can address that straight away. And if my two colleagues disagree with me on anything or wish to add or clarify anything beyond what I will be saying, please do so. As it is obvious from our decision itself, from the body of our decision, we are guided first and foremost with -- by our responsibilities under the Rules to make sure that you fulfil all your obligations, which basically means that all the rights of the accused under -- emerging from Rule 68(1) are fully respected. And in addition, our responsibility and to which we attach a great importance, to preserve to the best our abilities the integrity of these proceedings. This is what guides us. When we say "a thorough and complete search for Rule 68(1) material," we have chosen precisely those words because we want your search now, at this late stage of the proceedings when we have moved almost halfway through the Defence case, to be complete. How you conduct that research is your business. We are not going to tell you where to look for this material, whether you should go back through what you have searched already. That's your business. What concerns us, Mr. Wubben, and you will understand me completely, is that even in the process of elaborating the discussion on Mr. -- on the Defence motion, we started with one document, and in a space of two, three, four days, we ended up with more documents. And even at the very end, we were supposed not to have a second page of a document and at the end a second page appeared as well. So it's -- our concern is only one; that there is a full, thorough, and complete disclosure under Rule 68. We are definitely not going to tell you what to do or how to do that. That's your responsibility. What we want to know at the end of this exercise, on the 11th of November, is what you have done. Whether you have unearthed new documents, in which case, as per our decision, they have to be disclosed immediately and therefore, we would have a report on that. Of course, if you haven't unearthed anything, we would have a report on that, stating that. We would also require to note for future reference, because first we don't know how -- whether this is indeed the last case of violation that we have had. I mean, we might have, even after your fresh searches, we might end up with fresh documents. Right? That's number one. So we would want to know what you have found out, what's the result of your search, what kind of a search you did. We are -- it's none of our business where you searched except until you have concluded your search. Then you are supposed to tell us. And of course the results of such searches. I can't tell you more than that. We are only interested in a full and complete search precisely because it's your responsibility to do that, and that responsibility existed from even before the start of the trial. It existed even during the pre-trial -- the pre-trial stage, as you know. Because we are concerned about the rights of the accused to the maximum, and because we don't want a situation to obtain where, after having gone through a trial lasting a year plus, we end up with a possibility of having the whole proceedings endangered. So we have taken the steps that we consider necessary at this moment within our limits to ensure that there is full compliance with Rule 68(1). We can't control your searches, but we can impose on you the obligation to conclude a thorough and complete search. Now, where you search, I don't know because I don't know where your documents are. I mean, they can be in the electronic database. If you are happy with the searches you have conducted before, that's your business, but please do tell us at the end of this exercise what you have done, because it may be important later on for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have I been clear? If I haven't been clear, please come back to us and I will give you any further information, but I don't think I can go beyond what I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The second issue, if I may, is the order for immediate disclosure, and then I refer to the part "the ethnic cleansing by Serbs in the locations referred to in the indictment." Those locations, is it meant to be the relevant locations, all the locations meant in the indictment, I mean from Sarajevo up to Tuzla and so on, or is it meant the -- let's say 12 villages and hamlets attacked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You would notice immediately that the words "in the locations referred to in the indictment" are not our words but they reflect what is contained in the motion. That's number one. Number two, you would notice also that, in addition, we added after that "or which is in any other manner material to the Defence under Rule 68(1)." And we added that so that in your mind you would not have to worry whether there are any limitations as regards the locations. Our concern is this, and I repeat it, and I'm sure that with your experience you will understand me: Rule 68(1) deals with three aspects, and one is material which may suggest the innocence of the accused, material which may mitigate the guilt of the accused, or material which may affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence. Now, understandably, the motion dealt with Slobodan Misic. Understandably, also, because of the concern of the Defence, which the Trial Chamber shared -- shares, you could read in a very clear way from the motion itself that they were very much suspecting that there may be other Rule 68(1) material. They put it within the parameters of locations referred to in the indictment, which I agree with you could leave doubts exactly as to what it is meant. In order to make things clear that we really want the most thorough and the most complete search possible, we have included the words "which is in any manner material to the Defence under Rule 68(1)." I can assure, Mr. Wubben, that if you try and limit your search to the locations in whichever wide or narrow interpretation that you might choose to give it, you will probably end up not fulfilling your obligations under Rule 68(1) in a thorough and complete search, because it is beyond my reasonable understanding that exculpatory material, mitigating material, or material which affects the credibility of witness can only be found in material that relates to the locations referred to in the indictment. That material can exist elsewhere. In other words, it can exist in dossiers relating to other locations, dossiers relating to the war in general, dossiers coming from wherever. They don't need to be limited to the concept of locality, and that's precisely beyond that. When I drafted that, in my mind I had the question, "Is this ultra petita?" Does it go beyond what is asked by the Defence? But as I said, I was prepared to take the risk and decided, together with the agreement of my two colleagues, the way we did because we have got this big concern: We the ultimate responsibility of preserving the integrity of this case. God forbid that at the end of the day, if there is a conviction, because of course I don't know if there's going to be a conviction or not, but if there is a conviction, God forbid that at the end of the day, after all this travail, then we come up with further documents that should have been disclosed in 2003 or early in 2004 which were never disclosed and which will send the case back to trial or whatever the consequence will be. We are here to ensure that justice is done, and justice is done only if you fulfil your full -- your obligations to the full and the rights of the accused are protected and observed and respected to the full too. And we are responsible for that, and that is why we have decided the case -- the motion the way we have. I hope I have -- if you have further questions, please feel free. We have got another five minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour. If we might have additional questions, I will get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Incidentally, on this, do you wish to contribute or not? I mean, it was seeking clarification from the Trial Chamber, but if I have said anything which doesn't ring nicely to your ear, then please say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, just maybe one -- one thing, Your Honour, which is simply that our concern is -- is not that after a conviction that that conviction should be -- should be safe and that disclosure shouldn't mess that up. We say there should be a conviction under no circumstances. We simply want to have the documents so that we can effectively cross-examine. So I just -- I bridle slightly at the suggestion that the concern is that the proceedings will be endangered because -- the integrity of the proceedings, because, decoded, that means there will be a conviction, and we don't want that upset afterwards by disclosure breaches. We have a different perspective as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I can quite understand that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The other point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But your responsibilities are different from ours, Mr. Jones. I mean, we have a responsibility too to preserve the proceedings to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, I just -- I -- I hope I'm not reading Your Honours incorrectly, but I'm troubled by the suggestion that perhaps it's already in Your Honours' minds to convict and the disclosure concern is simply that the integrity of that proceedings shouldn't be jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why you are saying this because if you were following what I said, I said I obviously don't know how this case is going to end up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. Okay. I'm reassured, Your Honour. The second point is that I'm also concerned that in discussion of this topic, it always seems to be focused on searches as if disclosure is simply a matter of sitting in front of a terminal and entering search terms. There are analysts, there is, as I said before, institutional knowledge in the Office of the Prosecutor. The Rules refer to material in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor, so if there's an analyst who works in the Office of the Prosecutor or a trial attorney who has information which is exculpatory, in my submission, that resource needs to be tapped and it would be a violation if those people weren't consulted if it could be reasonably expected that they would have information which would be exculpatory. So we don't accept the suggestion that Rule 68 is simply a matter of entering search terms in a database and looking for documents. It's obviously more subtle than that. There are, as I say, there are analysts and there is a more intelligent way, I would submit, of approaching the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I fully agree with you, Mr. Jones. How, however, the Prosecution fulfils its obligation is the Prosecution's responsibility. We will only come in when we find out that there have been faults in the fulfillment of that obligation, as we have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as we will continue to do, but our hope is, and this is why we have given this decision the way it is, our hope is that this last motion of yours will indeed mark the last time that there has been a violation of Rule 68. This is what we are seeking to achieve, because that is our responsibility, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, and I want to share that hope and like to add to it that our perception of our disclosure obligation does not only stop with searches but an active approach. Whenever we receive new documents, new seizure of documents, we inform the Defence and we update them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll meet again on Monday in the morning. I can't remember which courtroom but it's definitely in the courtroom, with a new witness, who I suppose is here already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. He arrived last night, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And my information is that you need him for about six hours, six and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So be prepared. Six hours. And I'm told four hours from your part. Oh, it's Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson will respond to that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and indeed you are perceptive and correct, that I will no doubt be requiring the same amount of time, and of course we'll see how that goes with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So please make your calculations, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, as we go along next week, whether you will require another witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think our main concern is to definitely finish with that witness obviously before the break. That's the -- because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we're not sitting next Friday, and then the following week we are away, so obviously we would want to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. I misunderstood you. I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not by December, although one never knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's it. I wish you all a nice weekend and we will reconvene on Monday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
